calls.reason: The Li et al. study shows benchmark overlap rising in Common Crawl, and the Olmo3 study finds widespread soft contamination. Neither measures an increase over time in actual training on benchmarks across model cohorts, and nothing measures the financial stakes.

The Gu stress tests, ITBench's low completion rates and the METR slowdown all point to real limits. But the claim is hedged ('suggests') and judgmental, it sets no threshold for 'elusive', and METR's follow-up muddies the productivity evidence.

On the independent Remote Labor Index, the best agent fully automated only 2.5% of real multi-sector projects. OpenAI's GDPval figure is the company's own measure of win-or-tie on selected tasks, not of reliability. The cited 2023 papers measure exposure, not reliable completion.

Hendrycks et al. score GPT-5 at 57% of their AGI bar and report critical deficits and a 'brittle illusion' of generality, so current systems fall short on the framework he named. His summary of its criteria is a loose paraphrase, and he is a co-author of the paper.

Legg and Hutter support the historical emphasis on breadth, and the Leaderboard Illusion paper documents benchmark gaming. But the full Chen argument could not be read, and Chen explicitly appeals to flexible competence, so the charge of confusion is an interpretive dispute.

TechCrunch reports a profit-based AGI definition agreed by Microsoft and OpenAI, and Hendrycks et al. find a substantial gap for GPT-5 shortly before the post. Chen et al.'s contrary essay is an argument under a different standard, not a new measurement.
